lead: Transition diagrams, tables and the extended transition function let us see a finite automaton as a picture, as a spreadsheet and as a single function that reads whole words. The picture helps you trace a run by eye. The table lets a computer or a pen‑and‑paper test any input quickly. The extended function, often called δ̂, folds many single‑step moves into one step that works on strings. All three are used when you design a DFA, when you prove language properties, and when you implement a lexer for a programming language or a ticket‑booking bot.
prereq: You need: the definition of a DFA in Deterministic finite automata.

blocks.text: A transition diagram is a directed graph. Nodes are states. Arrows are labelled by input symbols. An arrow from q to p labelled a means the transition function δ(q,a)=p. The start state has an incoming arrow from nowhere. Accept states are drawn with a double circle.

items: Write down all states of the DFA.
For each state and each alphabet symbol, draw an arrow to the target state.
Mark the start state with an incoming arrow.
Mark accept states with double circles.
The diagram shows exactly the same information as the formal definition.
It is useful for visualising a run on a short input.

blocks.text: A transition table is a matrix. Rows list the states. Columns list the alphabet symbols. The entry at row q and column a is the state δ(q,a). The start state is noted separately. Accept states are listed in a separate set.

blocks.where: δ̂ is the extended transition function; q is a state; w = w₁w₂…wₙ is a string; each wᵢ is a symbol from the alphabet; δ is the single‑step transition function.

items: The table is easy to fill by hand for small DFAs.
A computer program can read the table and simulate the automaton in O(|w|) time.

blocks.text: The extended transition function δ̂ processes a whole string in one call. It is defined recursively.

items: Base case: δ̂(q, ε) = q, where ε is the empty string.
Recursive case: δ̂(q, xa) = δ( δ̂(q, x), a ), where x is a (possibly empty) prefix and a is the last symbol.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call δ̂ the extended transition function. Using δ̂ you can decide acceptance by checking whether δ̂(q₀,w) belongs to the set of accept states.

items: Do not reverse the order of symbols. The recursion works from left to right.
The function works for any deterministic automaton, not only for DFAs that accept binary strings.

figure.caption: The figure shows the four logical steps that the extended transition function performs on an input word.

spec.aria: Shows the steps of the extended transition function on an input string.

examples.question: Consider the DFA from chapter 2 with states q0,q1,q2, alphabet Σ={0,1}, start state q0 and accept state q2. The transition function is: δ(q0,1)=q1, δ(q1,1)=q2, δ(q2,0)=q2, and all other pairs lead to a dead state that is not accepting. Compute δ̂(q0,1101) step by step and state whether the string is accepted.
steps: Second symbol 1: δ̂(q0,11) = δ( q1 , 1 ) = q2.
Third symbol 0: δ̂(q0,110) = δ( q2 , 0 ) = q2 (self‑loop).
Fourth symbol 1: δ̂(q0,1101) = δ( q2 , 1 ) = dead (non‑accepting).
examples.answer: The string 1101 is rejected because the final state is not an accept state.

traps: Applying the symbols of the input string in reverse order when using the recursive definition of δ̂.
Confusing the dead state with an accept state because it may have a self‑loop on some symbol.
Reading the transition table column header as a state instead of as an input symbol.

quiz.q: What symbol is used to denote the extended transition function?
Explain why the extended transition function is defined recursively.
quiz.a: It processes a string one symbol at a time; the base case handles the empty string and the recursive case reduces a longer string to a shorter one by applying δ to the last symbol.

quiz.q: Given a DFA with δ(q0,0)=q1, δ(q1,1)=q2, δ(q2,0)=q0 and accept state q2, compute δ̂(q0,010).
quiz.a: δ̂(q0,0)=q1; δ̂(q0,01)=δ(q1,1)=q2; δ̂(q0,010)=δ(q2,0)=q0. Final state q0 is not accepting.

quiz.q: Fill the missing entry in the transition table: state q1, input 0 → __.
quiz.a: The entry is the state reached from q1 on symbol 0 as given by the DFA definition.

quiz.q: A student draws a transition diagram but forgets to double‑circle the accept state. How does this affect the language recognized?
quiz.a: The diagram will incorrectly suggest that strings ending in that state are not accepted. The recognized language will be missing all strings whose run ends in that state.

quiz.q: Two DFAs have identical transition tables but different start states. Can they recognize the same language? Justify.
quiz.a: Not necessarily. The start state determines the initial configuration. If the start states belong to different equivalence classes, the languages differ. Only if the two start states are equivalent (lead to the same set of accepted strings) will the languages be identical.

beyond: Not for the exam. Transition diagrams and tables are the basis of lexer generators used in compilers for Indian languages and in payment gateways that validate transaction codes. Researchers extend the extended transition function to weighted automata for speech recognition. The next step is to study nondeterministic automata, where the transition function maps to a set of states. Look for "ε‑moves" and the subset construction in the following chapter.
